---
title: "Ordinal Markov Random Field"
---

The ordinal Markov Random Field (MRF) is a graphical model for networks of
binary and ordinal variables. It is the default model in bgms.

## The model

For $p$ ordinal variables with observations
$\mathbf{x} = (x_1, \ldots, x_p)$, the ordinal MRF specifies the joint
distribution as:

$$
p(\mathbf{x}) \propto \exp\left(\sum_{i=1}^{p} \mu_{x_i}^{(i)} +
\sum_{i<j} \sigma_{ij} \, x_i \, x_j\right)
$$

where $\mu_{x_i}^{(i)}$ are category threshold parameters for variable $i$
(one per category above the lowest) and $\sigma_{ij}$ is the pairwise
interaction between variables $i$ and $j$.

A positive interaction $\sigma_{ij} > 0$ means that higher categories of
$x_i$ tend to co-occur with higher categories of $x_j$, conditional on all
other variables. The category thresholds control the marginal distribution
of each variable.

## Regular ordinal variables

By default, bgms treats ordinal variables as "regular": each category
above the lowest receives its own threshold parameter. This imposes no
constraint on the shape of the category distribution. Variables are
internally recoded to consecutive integers starting at 0.

For binary variables (two categories, coded 0 and 1), the model reduces to
the Ising model, a classical MRF for binary data. The single threshold
parameter controls the probability of category 1 relative to category 0.

## Blume-Capel variables

For ordinal variables with a natural baseline or reference category (e.g., a
"neutral" response), the Blume-Capel parameterization models category
thresholds as a quadratic function of distance from the baseline:

$$
\mu_c = \alpha \cdot (c - b) + \beta \cdot (c - b)^2
$$

where $c$ is the category, $b$ is the baseline category, $\alpha$ captures
the linear trend across categories, and $\beta$ captures the preference
toward or away from the baseline:

- $\beta < 0$: the model favors responses near the baseline category
- $\beta > 0$: the model favors extreme responses (far from the baseline)

Pairwise interactions between Blume-Capel variables use centered scores
$(c - b)$ rather than raw category values.

To use Blume-Capel variables, set `variable_type = "blume-capel"` and
provide the `baseline_category` argument:

```r
fit = bgm(x = data, variable_type = "blume-capel",
          baseline_category = 2, seed = 1234)
```

The `baseline_category` can be a single integer (applied to all variables)
or a vector of length $p$.

## Pseudolikelihood

The normalizing constant of the ordinal MRF is intractable for all but
the smallest networks. bgms uses a pseudolikelihood approximation: the
product of full conditional distributions replaces the joint distribution.
This makes estimation feasible for networks with many variables while
retaining consistent parameter estimates.

## Fitting an ordinal MRF

The ordinal MRF is the default model type. For ordinal or binary data,
call `bgm()` directly:

```r
fit = bgm(x = data, seed = 1234)
```

For Blume-Capel variables specifically:

```r
fit = bgm(x = data, variable_type = "blume-capel",
          baseline_category = 3, seed = 1234)
```

The output contains posterior summaries for both threshold parameters
(`posterior_summary_main`) and pairwise interactions
(`posterior_summary_pairwise`).

## References

Marsman, M., van den Bergh, D., & Haslbeck, J. M. B. (2025). Bayesian
analysis of the ordinal Markov random field. *Psychometrika*, 90(1),
146–182.
